name: ALG2-CDG (congenital disorder of glycosylation type Ii)

clinicalPearls: ALG2 encodes the endoplasmic reticulum alpha-1,3/1,6-mannosyltransferase that adds the second and third mannose residues to the lipid-linked oligosaccharide during early N-glycan assembly, placing it among the type I CDGs.
The classic presentation is an early-infantile epileptic encephalopathy, often with infantile spasms (West syndrome), profound developmental delay and central hypotonia.
Ocular involvement (iris or retinal coloboma, nystagmus), hepatomegaly and coagulation-factor deficiency are recognised systemic features.

A distinct allelic disorder, ALG2-related congenital myasthenic syndrome with tubular aggregates, causes limb-girdle fatigable weakness, so the same gene can produce a potentially treatable neuromuscular phenotype.
Carbohydrate-deficient transferrin shows a type I pattern (loss of whole glycan chains), but this may be subtle or normalise, so molecular confirmation is essential.
Lipid-linked oligosaccharide analysis in cultured fibroblasts shows accumulation of the truncated Man1-2 species, biochemically pinpointing the enzymatic block.
Neuroimaging commonly demonstrates hypomyelination with cerebral and cerebellar atrophy.
reference.pathophysiology: ALG2-CDG is an autosomal recessive type I congenital disorder of glycosylation caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in ALG2, which encodes the endoplasmic reticulum alpha-1,3/1,6-mannosyltransferase. This enzyme catalyses addition of the second and third mannose residues onto the dolichol-linked GlcNAc2-Man1 intermediate on the cytosolic face of the ER, an early committed step in building the Glc3Man9GlcNAc2 lipid-linked oligosaccharide that is transferred en bloc to nascent proteins. Deficient activity stalls oligosaccharide elongation, yielding truncated donor glycans, reduced N-glycosylation site occupancy and hypoglycosylation of numerous serum and membrane glycoproteins, which underlies the multisystem phenotype. Because ALG2 also supports the glycosylation required for stable neuromuscular junction function, certain hypomorphic variants instead manifest as a congenital myasthenic syndrome with tubular aggregates rather than the encephalopathic CDG picture.
additionalDifferentials: ALG1-CDG (CDG-Ik), which adds the first mannose and causes a clinically similar severe encephalopathy
ALG11-CDG (CDG-Ip), the neighbouring mannosyltransferase adding the fourth and fifth mannoses
PMM2-CDG (CDG-Ia), the prototypic type I CDG
Other genetic early-infantile epileptic encephalopathies unrelated to glycosylation
Congenital myasthenic syndromes with tubular aggregates (e.g. GFPT1, DPAGT1) for the allelic neuromuscular phenotype
additionalInvestigations: Serum transferrin isoelectric focusing / carbohydrate-deficient transferrin (type I pattern)
Whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing, or a targeted CDG gene panel, confirming biallelic ALG2 variants
Lipid-linked oligosaccharide profiling in cultured skin fibroblasts
Coagulation studies including fibrinogen and the natural anticoagulant factors
EEG to characterise the epileptic encephalopathy and identify hypsarrhythmia
MRI brain for hypomyelination and cerebral/cerebellar atrophy
For the myasthenic phenotype, repetitive nerve stimulation and muscle biopsy looking for tubular aggregates
redFlags: Intractable infantile seizures with developmental regression
Coagulopathy predisposing to bleeding or thrombosis, particularly before surgery
Feeding failure with failure to thrive
Fatigable weakness or respiratory compromise in the allelic myasthenic form
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is guarded, with the severe encephalopathic form associated with early morbidity and shortened survival. The allelic myasthenic phenotype may be milder and can respond to therapies that enhance neuromuscular transmission.
pitfalls: Transferrin testing can be normal or normalise beyond infancy, so a normal result does not exclude ALG2-CDG.
Overlooking that ALG2 variants can cause a treatable myasthenic syndrome mislabelled as a primary myopathy.
Attributing the coagulation abnormalities to hepatic disease alone rather than glycoprotein hypoglycosylation.
Assuming an abnormal transferrin pattern is diagnostic of PMM2-CDG without confirmatory genotyping.
references: Standard inborn errors of metabolism reference texts
Peer-reviewed reviews of congenital disorders of glycosylation
Clinical genetics and neurometabolic disease references
management: No disease-specific therapy for the encephalopathic form; supportive management through a metabolic multidisciplinary team
Anticonvulsant therapy for the epileptic encephalopathy, with corticotropin or vigabatrin considered for infantile spasms
For the allelic ALG2 congenital myasthenic syndrome, agents enhancing neuromuscular transmission such as the acetylcholinesterase inhibitor pyridostigmine
Correct coagulation factor and natural anticoagulant deficiencies around illness and procedures
Ophthalmology assessment for coloboma and nystagmus, with monitoring of hepatomegaly
Nutritional, feeding and developmental support for central hypotonia and delay
Genetic counselling and carrier testing for this autosomal recessive disorder
